title: Why Don't Satellites Fall Out of the Sky?
note: TEST FIXTURE ONLY: not fact-checked, not for upload. Used to check that a different video is NOT flagged as a duplicate.

sentences.text: Throw a ball and it curves back to the ground.
So why does a satellite, which is also pulled by gravity, stay up for years?
The surprising answer is that it is falling all the time.
Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on a very tall mountain.
Fire the ball faster and it lands farther away.
Fire it fast enough and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it drops.
The ball keeps falling but never reaches the ground.
Near the Earth, that speed is about 7.8 kilometres per second.
That is fast enough to cross India in about five minutes.
Go slower and the orbit dips into the air, where drag pulls the satellite down.
Higher orbits need less speed, because gravity is weaker farther away.
The Moon moves at only about 1 kilometre per second.
A geostationary satellite circles once a day, so it seems to hang over one spot.
Low satellites still brush the thin top of the atmosphere.
Each pass steals a little speed, and the orbit slowly shrinks.
That is why space stations fire their engines to climb back up.
A satellite stays up by moving sideways fast enough to keep missing the Earth.
It is not floating. It is falling around the planet.
